claims.text: CoCrFeMnNi-based high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings can be deposited by magnetron sputtering.
Typical sputtering conditions for these coatings yield homogeneous microstructures and standard interfacial characteristics.
Changing substrate bias, deposition rate, and deposition temperature can induce tailored residual compressive stresses at multilayer interfaces.
Changing sputtering parameters can promote atomically sharp, coherent interfaces in CoCrFeMnNi-based multilayers.
The engineered residual stress and interface characteristics can be made the only differences between optimized and baseline samples.
The proposed mechanism applies to CoCrFeMnNi coatings over approximately 300–500 K.
Residual compressive stresses elevate the local critical stress for dislocation nucleation.
Sharp, coherent interfaces act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Residual compressive stresses and coherent interfaces together reduce the rate of dislocation generation.
The combined residual-stress and interface effects impede dislocation glide.
Reduced dislocation generation and glide lower the accumulation of plastic strain over time under constant load.
Optimized coatings will have lower creep rates than homogeneous HEA coatings or multilayers lacking the engineered interfaces and residual stresses.
Optimized coatings will have increased yield thresholds relative to baseline coatings.
Optimized coatings will have higher activation energies for creep deformation.
Dislocation movement will begin later in optimized multilayers than in baseline coatings.
Optimized multilayers will exhibit fewer activated dislocation sources than baseline coatings.
At sufficiently high temperatures or extreme loads, deformation mechanisms other than interface-blocked dislocation motion can dominate.
Diffusion-controlled creep is an example of a mechanism expected to dominate at very high temperatures or extreme loading.
The separate quantitative contributions of residual stress and interface coherence remain uncertain because deposition changes may introduce confounding microstructural variations.

The hypothesis would be falsified if confirmed residual-stress and interface modifications fail to produce a statistically significant creep-rate reduction, a measurable yield-threshold increase, or the predicted reduction or delay in dislocation activity.
